claims.text: Premelting and melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are governed by competition between copper surface segregation and entropic stabilization of a homogeneous solid solution.
A copper-enriched liquid-like surface layer forms below the bulk melting temperature.
The liquid-like surface layer propagates toward the particle core as temperature increases.
The nanoparticles are initially solid, single-phase, and chemically homogeneous.
High-resolution in situ heating with structural imaging and compositional mapping can monitor premelting and melting progression.
A controlled comparison can be made against similarly sized bimetallic particles or HEA particles processed to minimize segregation.
Premelting may begin at approximately 0.8–0.9 times the aggregate melting temperature.
A copper-enriched surface layer has a lower local melting temperature than the particle interior.
The copper-enriched surface layer creates a gradient from a liquid-like disordered surface to an ordered solid core.
Elemental size mismatch and differing surface energies may induce additional local compositional deviations.
Copper has the lowest melting point among the constituent elements.
Differences in constituent melting points and surface energies cause copper to segregate preferentially to the nanoparticle surface at elevated temperature.
Copper surface segregation lowers the local surface melting temperature and causes early surface premelting.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the interior solid solution and delays complete melting.
Complete melting occurs after a critical premelted-layer thickness or degree of segregation is reached.
FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles will exhibit two-stage melting consisting of surface premelting followed by inward propagation of melting.
The premelting onset will be significantly below the bulk melting temperature.
Premelting will occur at a lower temperature or proceed more gradually than in the selected baseline nanoparticles.
The proposed behavior is most pronounced in high-surface-to-volume nanoparticles when diffusion permits segregation on the experimental timescale.
Larger particles or particles with slower diffusion may not show pronounced premelting.
